name: Foundations of Special Relativity
what: This subtopic introduces inertial reference frames, Einstein's two postulates, and the Michelson–Morley experiment. It explains why classical (Newtonian) mechanics breaks down at speeds approaching the speed of light.
why: Understanding the foundations gives students the conceptual basis for all the mathematical consequences of special relativity. Without a clear grasp of what a reference frame is and why the speed of light is constant, the equations for time dilation and length contraction have no meaning.

items.title: I can define an inertial reference frame and give examples
items.what: An inertial reference frame is one that is either stationary or moving at a constant velocity — it is not accelerating. Any frame moving at constant velocity relative to another inertial frame is also inertial.
items.why: Special relativity only applies to inertial frames. Identifying whether a frame is inertial or not is the first step in solving any relativity problem.
items.example: A train carriage moving at a steady 100 km/h on a straight track is an inertial frame. The same carriage while braking is a non-inertial frame because it is accelerating.

items.title: I can identify whether a given reference frame is inertial or non-inertial
items.what: A reference frame is non-inertial if it is accelerating — including speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction. A satellite in circular orbit is technically non-inertial because its direction is always changing.
items.why: Correct identification of frame type is needed before applying the postulates or equations of special relativity.
items.example: A rocket travelling at a constant 0.5c in a straight line is inertial. A rocket that is firing its engines and speeding up is non-inertial.

items.title: I can state Einstein's first postulate: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames
items.what: No inertial reference frame is special or preferred. Any experiment performed in one inertial frame will give the same result as the same experiment performed in any other inertial frame.
items.why: This postulate means that there is no absolute rest frame — you cannot perform an experiment inside a smoothly moving vehicle to determine whether you are moving or stationary.
items.example: A person on a smoothly moving train dropping a ball sees it fall straight down, just as someone standing on a platform would see a ball fall straight down. The physics is the same in both frames.

items.title: I can state Einstein's second postulate: the speed of light is constant for all observers
items.what: The speed of light in a vacuum, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, is the same for all observers regardless of the motion of the observer or the source of the light.
items.why: This postulate directly contradicts classical physics, where velocities add together. It is the reason time dilation and length contraction must occur — space and time must adjust so that every observer always measures light at c.
items.example: A rocket moving away from Earth at 0.5c turns on its headlights. An observer on Earth and the rocket crew both measure the light from those headlights travelling at exactly c, not at 1.5c or 0.5c.

items.title: I can explain why the null result of the Michelson–Morley experiment supports Einstein's theory
items.what: The Michelson–Morley experiment attempted to detect the luminiferous aether — a medium thought to carry light — by measuring changes in the speed of light in different directions relative to Earth's motion. The experiment found no difference at all (the null result).
items.why: The null result showed that light does not require a medium to travel through and that its speed is the same in all directions. This was direct evidence that the speed of light is constant for all observers, consistent with Einstein's second postulate.
items.example: If the aether existed, the two beams of light in the interferometer would return at different times (like a swimmer going with and against a current). But both beams always returned together, indicating the speed of light was the same in all directions.

items.title: I can compare Einstein's special relativity with the predictions of classical physics
items.what: Classical (Newtonian) physics assumes that velocities add directly and that time and length are absolute — the same for all observers. Special relativity replaces these assumptions: time and length are relative, and the speed of light is absolute.
items.why: Understanding this contrast shows where classical mechanics fails — at speeds approaching c — and why a new framework was needed.
items.example: Classical physics predicts that if a train moves at 0.5c and its headlights emit light, an observer on the ground measures that light at 1.5c. Special relativity says the observer measures it at c. Experiments confirm special relativity is correct.
